title: ‘Why Would You Bring That Up’ — NFL Analyst Brushes Off J.J. McCarthy Talk Amid Jameis Winston’s Back-to-Back Winning Performances
description: The New York Giants have made a bold decision that has shocked fans by acquiring J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings. The Giants’ quarterback situation seems to be getting more complicated with each passing day. The team’s starting quarterback, Jaxson Dart, suffered an injury that ultimately led to Jameis Winston taking over the starting job.
fullText:
The New York Giants have made a bold decision that has shocked fans by acquiring J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings. The Giants' quarterback situation seems to be getting more complicated with each passing day.

The team's starting quarterback, Jaxson Dart, suffered an injury that ultimately led to Jameis Winston taking over the starting job. The franchise then added McCarthy, creating questions about whether the former No. 10 overall pick could eventually challenge Winston for the starting role.

In a recent episode of NFL on CBS, analyst Pete Prisco shared his thoughts on the Giants' current situation and said:

"Well, first off, why would you even bring that up when you're coming off a game where Jameis Winston just won it? I don't understand the method in that. It doesn't make any sense. I get it. Jameis Winston is, and he talks about it, the Jameis Winston experience. No question. You're going to get three touchdowns and two picks, two horrible picks. "

"It's an up and down roller coaster ride. But why would you say that? He must have been directly asked about it. Why couldn't you just say, oh, he's been fine. He's picked up the offense. A plus. I mean, it's ridiculous. It makes no sense. What does that even mean? What he's had has like three or four practices. How do you get an A++ in three or four practices? You haven't even been in any game action yet. Practices are scripted, especially this part of the year. So it's just like, what does that mean? Maybe he's talking about he's got a full grasp of the offense already."

"Why would you even bring that up … coming off a game where Jameis Winston just won it?"@prisco after Matt Nagy said JJ McCarthy is an 'A+' in how he's coming along in the Giants' offense.#justfootball pic.twitter.com/hS1XSWOBvu

— NFL on CBS (@NFLonCBS) October 8, 2026

The comments highlight the unusual timing surrounding the Giants' decision to praise McCarthy publicly. Winston is currently producing results on the field, and his back-to-back winning performances have given the veteran an opportunity to strengthen his position as the team's starter.

While McCarthy's progress in practice could certainly be encouraging for the organization, it does not necessarily mean that he is ready to take over in a regular-season game. Practice performance can provide coaches with valuable information, but game action remains the ultimate test for any quarterback.

Winston's performances have also made the timing of the McCarthy discussion more interesting. If the veteran continues to lead the Giants to victories, the pressure to make a change could decrease. At the same time, the organization will likely want to evaluate McCarthy carefully after acquiring him and determine whether he can eventually become the team's long-term answer.

McCarthy comes with the potential to succeed, while Winston is proving his worth by leading the Giants to back-to-back wins. It will be interesting to see how the organization handles the situation as McCarthy continues to develop and Winston looks to maintain his momentum. The battle between potential and proven results could make the Giants' quarterback situation one of the most intriguing storylines to watch.

title: Browns HC Todd Monken reveals message he got after Jets passed on him
description: Todd Monken takes the Browns to MetLife Stadium on Sunday as a head coach, seven years after the Jets interviewed him for the same title and went another way. Ahead of the 1 p.m. ET kickoff, the first-year Browns coach recalled what he heard from the Jets once that 2019 search ended, in a clip […] The post Browns HC Todd Monken reveals message he got after Jets passed on him appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
Todd Monken takes the Browns to MetLife Stadium on Sunday as a head coach, seven years after the Jets interviewed him for the same title and went another way. Ahead of the 1 p.m. ET kickoff, the first-year Browns coach recalled what he heard from the Jets once that 2019 search ended, in a clip shared Friday by The 33rd Team's Ari Meirov.

Monken interviewed with New York in January 2019, when he was the Buccaneers' offensive coordinator. The Jets hired Adam Gase; the message Monken shared came from a member of the organization who was part of that interview process.

"Don't ever forget that you're a Mercedes when you look in the mirror. You can't control if they wanted a Lexus."

Monken added that it "doesn't matter how good of a Mercedes you are" when a team has a different car in mind, according to ClutchPoints.

It is a generous thing to tell a candidate on the wrong end of a decision, and it puts the outcome on the team's preference instead of the candidate's ability. It also leaves the candidate with a question that only gets answered years later, once both sides have a record to compare.

#Browns HC Todd Monken recalls what he was told after interviewing for the #Jets’ HC job in 2019, when they ultimately hired Adam Gase.

“Don’t ever forget that you’re a Mercedes when you look in the mirror. You can’t control if they wanted a Lexus.” https://t.co/l7Fsqx1qYS

— Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 9, 2026

Gase went 9-23 in two seasons. Robert Saleh followed and went 20-36 before he was fired five games into 2024, and interim coach Jeff Ulbrich went 3-9 the rest of that season. Aaron Glenn is 4-17 in his second year, a worse start than either Gase or Saleh had through the same number of games. Since the Jets passed on Monken, their head coaches have a combined record of 36-85.

After that interview, Monken's road ran straight to Cleveland. He became the Browns' offensive coordinator in 2019 under Freddie Kitchens, whose staff was fired after one season. He then called plays at Georgia and spent three seasons running Baltimore's offense, including Lamar Jackson's 2023 MVP season, before the Browns brought him back as HC.

His first team arrives at 3-1 with three straight wins. The Jets are 1-3. In last week's game they managed 157 yards of offense, committed 12 penalties and held the ball for just over 17 minutes.

Monken also praised the coach who holds the Jets job now. "I've always been a big AG fan. They play hard," Monken said. "He's wired the right way, and he'll have those guys ready to go."

title: Boosting U.S. oil supplies with Russian diesel unlikely to have impact on prices, experts say
description:
A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S.
fullText:
A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S. more than 300,000 tons of diesel. That would be followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November, then 4 million more tons at some point after that.

The deal marks a stark reversal of policy by the U.S., which from the start of Russia's war with Ukraine had banned imports of Russian oil, and comes at a time when the U.S. economy and consumers are being squeezed by a global rise in oil prices due to the eight-month-long U.S. war with Iran.

The price of diesel has shattered records in recent weeks, ratcheting up inflation for a broad swath of consumer goods.

The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22, according to motor club AAA. It averaged nearly $6.28 a gallon on Friday, up from almost $3.68 this time last year. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too.

Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That's because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.

Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel.

That's turned up the heat on Trump and the Republican Party to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The president's approval ratings on the economy have hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll released last week, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.

Energy policy experts on Friday expressed doubts that a boost in diesel supply from Russia will have a significant impact on oil prices, whether in the U.S. or globally.

"It's kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic," said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics.

"If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they'll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now," Lynch said.

And while the White House may be counting on this move to give some relief at the pump for U.S. truckers, ranchers and farmers who have been hit hard by rising diesel prices, that's not a given.

"The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe," Lynch said. "It just means that the oil is just going to be shuffled around and it's not really going to change the price globally or across the U.S."

If Russia, which in July moved to ban diesel exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries, now believes it is able to resume exports of diesel, then that will help stabilize global diesel prices, said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy.

However, prices are likely to remain elevated overall because a lot of refining capacity in the Middle East isn't available to the world market due to the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz from the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.

"Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels," Sternoff said. "So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them."

While the deal between Trump and Putin probably won't have much of an impact on prices for diesel consumers in the U.S., it will benefit Russia, said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

That's because Russia is trying to offload its summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months, Seigle noted.

"I don't think it'll be enough to materially lower prices in the United States or Europe, but it does certainly let Moscow off the hook in terms of revenue squeeze," he said.

title: Russian strikes kill 12 in Ukraine a day after Trump's diesel deal with Putin
description:
— Russian strikes killed at least 12 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, a day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel that Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Zelenskyy said Saturday. At least 14 people were wounded in the attack.
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian strikes killed at least 12 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, a day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel that Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow's war in Ukraine.

Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Zelenskyy said Saturday. At least 14 people were wounded in the attack.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.

Trump said Friday he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X.

He said the attacks show Moscow understands "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities," adding that "different signals are needed."

Trump had been set to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.

Instead, the American leader announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.

"Trump has once again shown his true face," said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. "He didn't care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he's interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay."

"Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He's got an election coming up soon," Petrenko said. "So he needs to emphasize to his voters that gasoline will be cheap. But it won't be effective."

For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement "didn't really come as a surprise."

"Trump has been working with Putin for a long time," she told The Associated Press.

Trump's announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.

In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal on Friday, Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He framed it as an investment in the war that could prolong it.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelenskyy called it "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners."

Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

Bela Szandelzsky in Kyiv, Ukraine, contributed to this report.

title: Trump says Nobel panel not awarding him peace prize leaves 'indelible stain' on Norway
description:
President Donald Trump lamented the Norwegian Nobel Committee choosing not to award him with its annual peace prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.”
Speaking at a rally to boost New York Republicans in Syracuse, Trump listed off all of the accomplishments in office he believes have earned him the right to win the Nobel Peace Prize, including efforts to end or prevent conflicts in Africa and Asia and for having “saved more lives than anyone in history.”
Earlier Friday, the committee awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African legal pioneer who led a U.N. panel that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
fullText:
President Donald Trump lamented the Norwegian Nobel Committee choosing not to award him with its annual peace prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.”

Speaking at a rally to boost New York Republicans in Syracuse, Trump listed off all of the accomplishments in office he believes have earned him the right to win the Nobel Peace Prize, including efforts to end or prevent conflicts in Africa and Asia and for having “saved more lives than anyone in history.”

Earlier Friday, the committee awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African legal pioneer who led a U.N. panel that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

“I’ve never heard of the person,” Trump said. “I know a lot of people. I never heard of this particular person, but congratulations, anyway. … The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.”

“And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump continued. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are antidemocracy and really enemies of civilization, and we will not forget Norway. That you didn’t give this prize with the greatest record in history.”

The president added that he should have received eight Nobel Peace Prizes for his efforts because he claimed to have ended eight ongoing conflicts. The president did not make mention of the war in Ukraine, which has raged on through his presidency as his administration has failed to bring the conflict to an end. And in the Middle East, the president earlier this year launched a war with Iran that is ongoing.

Trump said the committee’s choice to award the prize to Pillay “is just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country.”

Throughout his second term, the president has made clear his ambition to secure a Nobel Peace Prize, and his allies have said he deserves it for efforts to end the war in Gaza in addition to other conflicts. Earlier this year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 winner, offered to share her prize with him as she sought his support for her efforts in Venezuela after the Trump administration removed former President Nicolás Maduro from power.

After learning of her award at a law gathering in Germany on Friday, Pillay joked to the crowd: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

The president was in Syracuse to boost the candidacy of GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman and state Republicans. He shouted out Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for state attorney general too, before attacking sitting state Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat he has often clashed with.

“And on Election Day, New Yorkers should tell both [Gov. Kathy] Hochul and that disgusting Letitia dog — she’s a dog — you’re fired. Get the hell out of here.”

The Trump administration has so far failed multiple times in its efforts to prosecute James, who spearheaded an investigation into his business dealings that led to a state judge ruling he had conspired to manipulate his net worth and ordering him to pay a fine of more than $350 million. The fine was later thrown out on appeal by a state court.

“Donald Trump is in Syracuse supporting the only attorney general candidate who clerked for Brett Kavanaugh, the man who ended Roe v. Wade,” a James campaign spokesperson said in response to the president’s comments. “The contrast is crystal clear and we welcome it.”

fullText:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - Isaias weakened to a post-tropical cyclone on Saturday, having rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the ‌Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic ‌season, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.

The post-tropical cyclone, crossing over southern Alabama ​after making landfall earlier near Destin, Florida is about 55 miles (89 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), the agency added.

Isaias is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC ‌said.

The center warned of possible ⁠storm surges, urban and river flooding and flash floods across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and ⁠the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.

A risk for tornadoes will also persist overnight across the Florida Panhandle and north Florida into southern Georgia, while the tornado threat will continue on Saturday ​across ​parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia, and the Carolinas, ​the agency said.

Alabama's emergency management agency ‌said the hurricane has downed trees and power lines, making travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning.

"Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. "These road closures will remain in effect until conditions are deemed safe for travel."

President Donald Trump, asked ‌about hurricane preparations, told reporters outside the White ​House, "We're watching it very closely, the hurricane," adding ​that it was "under control."

More than 430,000 ​people in Florida and nearly 297,000 in Alabama lost power as ‌the storm hit shore, according to power ​outage tracking firm PowerOutage.us.

"Emergency ​declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.

Florida's ​emergency services urged residents ‌to shelter in place and watch for hurricane conditions across the north of ​the state.

title: Trump takes lawsuit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
description:
President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year's election by linking his campaign to ‌Russia. 
   The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers ‌for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions. 
   In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the ​Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida. 
   Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia.
fullText:
Oct 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year's election by linking his campaign to ‌Russia.

The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers ‌for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.

In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the ​Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.

Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged "racketeering" and a "conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood," among other claims.

Trump defeated Clinton in that election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021.

US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, ‌and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller ⁠documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a "hoax."

Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year's ⁠election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.

US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump's lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump's lawsuit to a "two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him."

Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and ​his ​lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the ​sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended "to dishonestly ‌advance a political narrative." The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a "continuing pattern of misuse of the courts."

Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained "knowingly false" factual allegations and asserted "frivolous" legal theories.

The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge's rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.

"Many of Trump's and Habba's legal arguments were indeed frivolous," the 11th Circuit stated.

In court papers, lawyers for Trump and Habba have said that the decisions by the lower courts are having a "profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole."

Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia "interfered in the 2016 presidential election in ‌sweeping and systematic fashion," but stated that "the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign ​conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities."

Mueller said in his report that he ​found "numerous links" and that the Trump campaign "expected it would benefit" from Russia's effort ​to tilt the ballot in Trump's favor.

Trump's then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential ‌missteps by the FBI.

In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the ​FBI lacked "actual evidence" to investigate Trump's 2016 presidential ​campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump's political opponents to fuel the probe.

Trump's Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. ​A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor ‌who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed.

Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of ​the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump's campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, ​all of which Trump denied.

title: Erik Prince's private forces ambushed in Congo with former UFC fighter among wounded
description:
Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said.
The frontline clash ‌shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which ‌also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously helped Congo's army secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east.
A veteran special operator reported on ​his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported.
fullText:
DAKAR, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said.

The frontline clash ‌shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which ‌also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously helped Congo's army secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east.

A veteran special operator reported on ​his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported.

The attack in South Kivu on September 17 left about 20 dead and wounded, two sources working with Congo's government said. The dead included at least seven Congolese and a former member of New Zealand's Special Forces, while the wounded included Kennedy and another foreign contractor, the sources said.

A Vectus Global representative declined to comment. The company has not previously suffered casualties in Congo, a source with direct ‌knowledge of the operation said.

One of the sources who works for ⁠Congo's government said that Rwandan forces backing the M23 rebels may have surprised them by tracking a drone used for surveillance operations to their location.

Spokespeople for the Congolese and Rwandan governments and for the M23 did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Kennedy, the former mixed martial arts fighter, survived the attack ⁠with three gunshot wounds to the leg, three sources said, and is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in the suburbs of Washington.

Kennedy has a popular podcast channel and millions of followers on social media. Trump is a fan of UFC, hosting fights at the White House this year.

The US State Department and Walter Reed declined to comment. Kennedy's parents did not respond to requests for comment.

A ​Congolese ​security source, who said some 20 people were wounded and killed in the attack, added that villagers were likely ​among the casualties as well. Reuters spoke to at least 10 sources ‌either with direct knowledge of the attack or briefed on the outcome.

PRINCE TOOK EXPANDED ROLE IN CONGO'S CONFLICT

Prince's initial mandate in Congo was to secure and improve revenue collection from the country's vast mineral reserves, which have been plundered for decades, fuelling relentless conflict in the east.

But in January and early February, his forces deployed to Uvira after Washington helped broker a deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from the strategic town.

The size of Prince's forces in Congo is unclear.

One of the sources with direct knowledge of the attack said the Vectus team was travelling between locations when the ambush took place and its sophistication suggested Rwandan forces were involved.

"It reinforces the need for DRC sovereignty to be restored. It's an incredibly dangerous place right now," the source said.

Two ‌other sources said the ambush was carried out by the Rwandan military.

Prince is the founder of now-defunct ​private military firm Blackwater, some of whose members were pardoned in 2020 for killing Iraqi civilians.

The State Department has ​said it does not have any contracts with Prince in Congo, though US officials have ​said they plan to work more closely with Vectus Global in Haiti.

The deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from Uvira was part of wider agreements brokered ‌by the Trump administration to try to end the conflict in eastern ​Congo.

Kennedy, a father of four, has posted ​his views on politics, culture, fitness and more on social media. He also runs a popular YouTube podcast in which he interviews UFC fighters, veterans, cultural disruptors and others.

He has often posted about his family, including four young children. In late August, he posted about having "incredible conversations about what being a man means and what sacrifice really looks like" ​with his son. He did not disclose details about his upcoming ‌trip to Congo.

The United Nations and Western powers say Rwanda backs M23, even exercising command and control over the group. Rwanda denies this. Fighting in the decades-long ​conflict flared early last year, with M23 fighters making rapid gains in the east, which is rich in tantalum, gold, lithium and other minerals.

(Additional reporting by Clement ​Bonnerot in Dakar and David Lewis in London; Writing by Jessica Donati; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

title: NI debut 'something I thought had passed' - Elmore
description: Northern Ireland's World Cup hopes may have all but come to an end against Portugal, but for Kess Elmore the 4-0 defeat marks the start of a long-awaited international journey.
fullText:
Northern Ireland's World Cup hopes may have all but come to an end against Portugal, but for Kess Elmore the 4-0 defeat marked the start of a long-awaited international journey.

After a ruthless first-half display from Portugal in Larne gave them a comfortable advantage at the break, Elmore's half-time introduction made an impact for Northern Ireland, who were much improved after the interval.

Elmore was a surprise call-up for the play-off double header against world number 22-ranked Portugal after having been involved in an NI training camp in 2021 and thought her chance to pull on a green shirt was over.

"I wasn't expecting Michael to call me. It was in the back of my mind, but definitely something that I kind of thought had passed," Elmore said.

"I've played in a lot of teams with a lot of different formations, tactics and, over the years, I have gained a real understanding of the game. So, hopefully I can bring a bit of that experience into the squad because we do have a young squad and I bring an attacking presence.

"It's great to have those experiences under my belt because now going into these games, I feel pretty confident in what I can do and what I can bring."

Elmore's debut came on a difficult evening for Northern Ireland, who struggled against a clinical Portugal side at Inver Park.

However, Elmore gave her side a different dimension to their attack with the debutant bringing energy and movement in the final third.

"I had no idea whether I'd make my debut or not, but I got told at half-time that I'd be coming on and, obviously, that was really nice to hear," she continued.

"I just wanted to come on and bring energy and work for the team. Portugal had a lot of momentum in the first half, so I kind of wanted to shift that in our favour and I feel like the second half was a lot better.

"So, I'm happy that I could contribute to that. We knew it was going to be a very defensive game for us but huge respect to Portugal and what they can do."

While the Northern Ireland fans will feel a lot of disappointment after the four-goal defeat, Elmore's performance offered an encouraging glimpse of what she could bring to the young squad.

She was also just one of three players who earned their first cap against Portugal, underlining McArdle's determination to wide his options and build depth within the squad.

Despite Elmore normally playing on either the wing or in midfield for Sparta Prague, she spent much of her time at Inver Park leading the NI line as a lone striker.

For a player who has already tested herself on some of European football's biggest club stages, including the Champions League and Europa League this year, Elmore added this was another challenge she would embrace.

"That was the first time playing centre-forward for a very long time since university.

"I like any of the attacking positions and anywhere attacking, I'm happy to play. I mean, anywhere the team needs me, I'm happy to be there."

Manager McArdle also believes the England youth international can add to the squad, who will now travel to Portimao on Tuesday (19:45 BST) but face a tough task.

"I think with Kess come on, obviously making her debut as well, I think that brings a nice energy," McArdle said.

"I'm grateful that we've all seen Kess because you'll see what I see now. There is someone here who can add to the group and give us something going forward and in the final third, so delighted that she's gone on the pitch."

title: Delight for Scotland's Cuthbert after long summer of recovery
description: Erin Cuthbert expresses joy and relief at making her first appearance of the season in Scotland's impressive 2-0 win over Czech Republic.
fullText:
Erin Cuthbert expressed joy and relief at making her first appearance of the season in Scotland's impressive 2-0 win over the Czech Republic.

Chelsea captain Cuthbert, 28, is yet to feature at club level this season following a knee injury and came on as a substitute in Pardubice. Fellow sub Claire Emslie finished superbly for the Scots' second after captain Caroline Weir's stunning opener.

"It's so good," Cuthbert told BBC Scotland.

"It's been such a long summer. It's always great to come on and play for my country again - I'll never take it for granted when I get a serious injury.

"I'm just glad to get back on a football pitch. The relief, the amount of self-doubt that you have, the amount of stress - am I going to be back to the same level, how am I going to perform, is my knee going to be alright? All those things run through your head.

"It was a bad one. I was in crutches and a brace for the best part of a month. I lost a fair amount of muscle and over the summer I was trying to rebuild all of that again.

"It's been a really, really hard journey."

Emslie scored her first goal since becoming a mum, with her son and mother attending the game in Pardubice.

"I'm incredibly proud of her," Cuthbert said of Emslie. "I have an enormous amount of respect for her. Everything's just so impressive - to be a mum, to play at the highest level."

The Czech Republic were given a late reprieve when the award of a penalty was overturned but, soon after, Cuthbert was "flabbergasted" a late challenge on her in the box did not result in a spot-kick.

And while Cuthbert was "delighted" with the win, she cautioned that 2-0 can be a "dangerous" lead.

"We're a good team and when we play on the front foot, we can hurt teams," she added. "The best form of attack is defence."

title: Raphinha's brilliant Barcelona start interrupted by injury concerns
description: Raphinha will miss Barcelona's next two fixtures after returning from international break with an injury.
fullText:
Raphinha has made a phenomenal start to the season for Barcelona, cementing his status as one of Europe's most formidable attackers.

The 29-year-old has scored 14 times and provided three assists as the Spanish champions have racked up eight successive wins in all competitions.

His performances have been so impressive that his omission from the 30-man Ballon d'Or shortlist prompted debate, with some arguing his form warranted greater recognition among the game's elite.

Yet, just as Raphinha appeared ready to take his game to another level, injury concerns have interrupted his momentum and he looks set to miss Barcelona's next two fixtures.

Facing a demanding run of fixtures, including meetings with Paris St-Germain and Real Madrid this month in the Champions League and La Liga, keeping the Brazilian fit could prove just as important as making the most of his remarkable goalscoring form.

Raphinha withdrew from international duty with a right thigh injury after he was substituted at half-time in Brazil's match against Australia.

"The tests show something," Barcelona boss Hansi Flick told the media.

"It's not a serious injury, but we have to be careful because he had three injuries last year, and we have to take care of him."

Flick defended Raphinha's decision to want to play for Brazil.

"It's the national team and everyone wants to play for their national team," he said. "That's Raphinha's mentality. Always give 100%."

Although the setback does not appear to be major, the timing has not been ideal.

"We must reflect on whether it was necessary for him to play in Australia, travelling so many thousands of kilometres," added Flick. "It's incredible. They have to choose friendly matches and in Europe it is not possible because of the Nations League."

With tough tests to come, Flick will want all his leading attackers available and hope even a short spell on the sidelines won't disrupt Raphinha's rhythm.

The situation has also presented Flick with a familiar dilemma. At the start of the season, there were concerns Barcelona had no established number nine after veteran Poland striker Robert Lewandowski left the club.

Raphinha has mainly been playing as a false nine this season, rather than his usual role on the wing and the team have looked unstoppable.

They sit top of La Liga, five points clear of Atletico Madrid and Real Betis, with Real Madrid a point further back in fourth place, and thrashed Feyenoord 5-1 in their Champions League opener. With 36 goals scored and eight conceded, they've been dominant at both ends of the pitch.

For now, fellow Brazilian Gabriel Jesus - a deadline-day arrival from Arsenal in September - is likely to cover Raphinha's absence for the next two matches against Getafe on Saturday and then the European trip to Galatasaray.

Flick, though, has huge depth in his Barcelona squad, and Anthony Gordon, Dani Olmo and Karim Adeyemi could all play as a false nine if necessary.

Raphinha's numbers tell an impressive story, but his contribution to Barcelona extends beyond the stats.

He is the team captain and has become a central figure in their aggressive, high-intensity approach, combining direct attacking play with relentless pressing and a willingness to work for the team.

His finishing has become a defining feature of his game. Rather than relying on creating chances for others, Raphinha has developed into a consistent source of goals himself and Barcelona's performances so far have reflected that influence.

The former Leeds United player has been a key factor in why Flick's side have looked so threatening in the final third and could equal the 2013-14 record for the best start to a La Liga season if they beat Getafe for an eighth straight league win.

Raphinha, though, will be determined to avoid a repeat of last season, which demonstrated how quickly fitness problems can complicate the club's plans and ambition.

He was restricted to 33 appearances, with recurring fitness issues and a hamstring injury contributing to his absences.

Raphinha played seven times in the Champions League but, crucially, was missing as his side went out in the quarter-finals with defeat by Atletico Madrid.

His tally of 21 goals helped deliver the league title and he scored twice in a standout performance in the Spanish Super Cup final against Real Madrid.

Given his importance, the temptation for Flick to rush Raphinha back will be understandable and Barca will hope this is a brief interruption rather than the beginning of another frustrating injury cycle.

title: Crocker sets sights on route back to the top
description: Lewis Crocker is looking forward and not back at his world title defeat by Liam Paro as he prepares for his return against Owen Cooper in December at Belfast's 02.
fullText:
The flight home from Australia in June was a little longer for Lewis Crocker as he pondered his defeat by Liam Paro in his first defence of the IBF welterweight title.

A storming finish by the Belfast man was not enough to turn things around as all three judges gave Paro a 115-113 decision and the Australian realised his dream of becoming a two-weight champion.

Crocker grew into that fight and seemed on the brink of finding a finish in the late rounds, but Paro held on and Crocker lost his grip on the title he won last September in Belfast's Windsor Park against Paddy Donovan - his record slipping to 22 wins with one loss.

"Shoulda, woulda, coulda," is how the 29-year-old reflects on that night in Brisbane - one in which he was so near yet so far away, yet his first career defeat has not dented confidence, but only served to fuel his desire to rise again.

"I got beaten on a very close decision in a world title fight against a two-weight world champion," Crocker told BBC Sport NI.

"I gained experience from it anyway, and at 29 I've still got plenty more for whatever opportunity is coming.

"I felt like I had him hurt a lot of times and he was holding, if he gets a point taken off then I win the fight. Shoulda, woulda, coulda...

"That was a long fight back, but I'm over it because I know I'm right there. My main focus now is going to be a two-time world champion."

The first step on that quest takes place at The O2 in Belfast on 19 December when Crocker faces former English champion Owen Cooper [12-2] on the undercard of the Anthony Cacace v Nick Ball world super-featherweight title clash.

Perhaps it's further evidence that the old promotional cold war in British boxing is over as Crocker - promoted by Matchroom - will box on a Queensberry card and he is delighted to be back on home turf, promising fans a "Christmas Crocker" on the night.

That his first world title defence didn't take place in his home city instead of over 10,000 miles away on the east coast of Australia could be a source of consternation.

However, Crocker has always held a philosophical view of it all, insisting the opportunity to defend a world title in Australia is "something you'd dream of as a kid".

Still, it is good to be home as he embarks upon a route back to the top and while opportunities may present themselves in 2027, Crocker is not looking past the challenge of 26-year-old Cooper who will see this as his golden ticket.

"It would have been great to have a first defence in Belfast, but ultimately it doesn't matter - there's still two men getting into the ring," Crocker reasoned.

"It's good to be back in Belfast anyway, and get on the road to two-time world champion.

"More than anything now, I want to be a two-time world champion and we've a great plan ahead but I'm not looking past Owen, because he's a great fighter and I'm expecting a really tough test."

Crocker's old foe Paddy Donovan is front of the queue to face Paro, while the welterweight division has come alive once again with some of the sport's biggest names in Ryan Garcia [WBC], Teofimo Lopez [WBA] and Devin Haney [WBO] holding the other titles.

A second shot at a title at Windsor Park where he won his first against Donovan "would be great" but whomever and wherever, Crocker would be happy to take.

"There are four world titles out there, so any one of them [would be great]," he continued.

"[I plan to get] back on track and push towards it, but as I say, Owen's my main focus right now."

title: Wales must improve in World Cup bid - Wilkinson
description: Rhian Wilkinson accepts Wales must raise their standards after they scrape to a 1-0 victory in their Women's World Cup play-off semi-final in Albania.
fullText:
Rhian Wilkinson accepted Wales must raise their standards after they scraped to a 1-0 victory in their Women's World Cup play-off semi-final in Albania.

Wales have the upper hand going into Tuesday's second leg in Llanelli after Ezmiralda Franja's first-half own goal gave them victory in Shkoder.

But Wilkinson's team were fortunate to triumph against a team who sit 37 places below them in the Fifa rankings after Albania created the game's best chances.

"We stuck with it. [It was a] resilient performance. Not our best, but equally, we learned to win on hard days, and today it wasn't our best," the Wales head coach said.

"Coming home with [the win] is great. We're halfway there.

"We need to make sure we take care of business at home but equally push our standards a bit."

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final second leg

Tuesday, 13 October at 19:15 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Wilkinson had set a clean sheet as Wales' primary target in Albania and her players delivered on that score, albeit in fortuitous fashion.

While Wales' attacking threat was limited, Franja, Fortesa Berisha and Megi Doci all came close for the home side.

Albania's failure to convert one of their opportunities meant that just as had been the case in their three away games in the group stage of World Cup qualifying, Wales claimed a positive result despite being frustrated with aspects of their performance.

"I didn't think we defended overly well today to be honest, but what we did do is we never quit," Wilkinson added.

"I do think I've been in this job long enough to have seen that growth with this team, that we're finding ways to stick in the game.

"And we've got to be happy with that right now because, again, we're away from home and in an environment where they made it really tough."

Wales thumped Albania 4-0 in Wrexham on their way to winning Group B4, during which they thumped Montenegro in Llanelli and claimed a rousing 3-1 success against the Czech Republic in Cardiff.

They return to Parc y Scarlets hoping another dominant home performance will send them through to a two-legged play-off final in December.

Wales beat Albania in World Cup play-off first leg

"Albania will feel like they were right in this game and they were," Wilkinson said.

"So we've got to make sure that we match their energy and take advantage of the stretch in the game that they're going to give us because they're going to go for it.

"It's another battle. I'm confident in my team, but we've got to be ready to fight because definitely Albania will be."

Should they progress, Wales look likely to face Norway after Gemma Grainger's team won 2-0 in Romania on Friday.

Even if Wales topple the Norwegians, who are ranked 14th in the world, they may then have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs next February to secure a place at next summer's World Cup in Brazil.

title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
description:
Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase
The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.
Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase

The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.

Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.

The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.

The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.

Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.

Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.

They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.

She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.

“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”

A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.

“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.

“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”

A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.

A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.

“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.

Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.

Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.

That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.

The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.

Watson was approached for comment.

title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
description:
George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.
The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field

The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.

The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.

The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.

“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.

In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.

“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.

Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”

He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.

Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030.

“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.

“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.”

Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”

Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.

Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.

In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology.

Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”

“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.

“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.

Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”

He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”

Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards.

“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

title: Palmer signs new Chelsea contract until 2034
description: Cole Palmer signs a new Chelsea contract on improved terms until 2034, one of the longest active deals in the Premier League.
fullText:
Cole Palmer has signed a new Chelsea contract on improved terms until 2034.

The England international, 24, was already under contract until 2033 but is being rewarded for his performances following his emergence as one of Chelsea's key attacking players.

He is also increasingly viewed as a dressing-room leader behind the scenes.

The deal leaves Palmer on one of the longest contracts in the Premier League, with only Manchester City's Erling Haaland and Chelsea team-mates Joao Pedro and Geovany Quenda also contracted to 2034.

"Chelsea means a lot to me and I think the club is going in the right direction, so I'm delighted to sign and I'm obviously very happy," said Palmer.

"Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of confidence so it was only right to sign.

"Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions. I feel like we win major trophies here consistently and I want to be a part of that and play a big role in it too."

Palmer signed his previous contract only two years ago having joined in a £42.5m move from Manchester City in 2023.

The renewal is the latest in a series of contract extensions at Chelsea designed to reward established and emerging players while maintaining the club's wage structure.

Joao Pedro also signed a new contract until 2034 in August, followed by Pedro Neto signing a new six-year contract last month.

Palmer has developed a strong understanding with the Brazil forward, while also rekindling his on-pitch partnership with his "best friend in football", Morgan Rogers, during the early stages of Xabi Alonso's reign as manager.

He was one of the few people privy to Chelsea's negotiations to sign Rogers from Aston Villa for a club-record £117m fee this summer.

Palmer has scored four goals and provided two assists in seven matches this season.

It represents a return to form for Palmer after suffering a niggling groin issue throughout last season, when he admitted he had played through the problem even though he "probably shouldn't have done".

Ultimately, his lack of availability led to his omission from England's World Cup squad over the summer, having previously sought specialist advice on whether surgery was required.

Palmer has played more minutes than any Chelsea player this season but missed England's recent international break, prompting Thomas Tuchel to say he "misses too many opportunities".

Alonso confirmed Palmer is expected to be available for Saturday's game against Bournemouth and insisted he remains committed to playing for England.

"Absolutely. He's committed, but he needs to be fully fit to play," Alonso said.

"And when he's fully fit, he will enjoy his minutes. We need him in that moment. The club and the national team.

"He trained over the past week and has been feeling better, but we didn't want to rush him."

Alonso's side are 10th in the table after five matches, having conceded 12 goals.

title: All Blacks power past Australia to retain Bledisloe Cup
description: New Zealand retain the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year as they power past Australia to extend their remarkable unbeaten run at Eden Park.
fullText:
Tries: Lakai, Vaai, Roigard, Taylor, Carter, Moorby, Jordan Cons: McKenzie (6) Pens: McKenzie

Tries: Wright, Wilson, Nasser Cons: Lonergan (2)

New Zealand retained the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year as they powered past Australia to extend their remarkable unbeaten run at Eden Park.

The All Blacks have not lost at the venue since 1994, with a dominant second-half display increasing their unbeaten run in Auckland to 54 Tests.

Australia remained in touch at half-time at 17-14 down but New Zealand blew the visitors away after the break, scoring five tries.

Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Will Jordan all scored as fly-half Damian McKenzie kicked 15 points to help the All Blacks retain the trophy which is contested annually between the two nations.

Victory halted a three-match losing streak for the All Blacks after the 3-1 series defeat by world champions South Africa this summer.

Defeat for the Wallabies was their first since head coach Les Kiss succeeded Joe Schmidt in July, ending their six-game unbeaten run.

Australia were looking for their first win at Eden Park since 1986 and went ahead after controlling the early stages through full-back Tom Wright's try.

New Zealand responded strongly, and inspired by scrum-half Roigard's searching kicks, turned the match around with tries from Lakai and Vaa'i.

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson scored a try to keep New Zealand at arm's length, but the All Blacks moved through the gears in the second half.

Roigard grabbed a try for himself shortly after the break, before Taylor, Carter, Moorby and Jordan went over as Australia struggled to hold back the hosts' waves of attack.

Josh Nasser added a late try for the visitors, but the match was well beyond their reach by that point.

The second match of the two-Test series takes place in Sydney at the Accor Stadium on 17 October.
